subtitle: Learn how Afghan Minnesotans came to the state, the languages and peoples within the community, and how to offer respectful, well-matched service without guessing about any one person.
audience: For all DHS and DSD employees, including case managers, eligibility and policy staff, communications and data staff, who want shared, accurate context before working with Afghan individuals, families and community partners.

lessons.title: From earlier arrivals to the evacuation: how Afghan Minnesota grew
objectives: Explain how the 2021–2022 response and 2024 arrival figures describe different groups and periods.
Distinguish humanitarian parole, Special Immigrant Visa and refugee pathways at a basic level.
Explain why immigration status questions belong with the responsible program or legal service, not with general staff curiosity.
Identify one limit of state arrival data.
lessons.teaching:
Afghanistan has lived through more than four decades of war and upheaval: the Soviet invasion in the late nineteen-seventies, the civil war that followed, the first period of Taliban rule, the long U.S.-led military presence, and the Taliban's return to power. Each period pushed people out of the country. Minnesota’s Afghan community includes people who arrived before 2021 and people who came during and after the emergency evacuation that followed the Taliban’s return in August 2021. Their histories and present circumstances differ.

In the months after the evacuation, Minnesota organized a rapid health response for newly arriving Afghans. A peer-reviewed account describes 1,260 Afghan evacuees across 386 families resettling in Minnesota from October 1, 2021, through February 17, 2022. Those figures describe the group served during that response, rather than all Afghan Minnesotans. The Minnesota Refugee Health Report for 2024 lists 603 primary arrivals from Afghanistan, after Somalia and Ukraine in its country totals. Keep the reporting year and arrival category with a number; these historical figures do not describe the current population of a county.

Afghan Minnesotans arrived through several pathways. Many evacuees arrived in 2021 with permission to stay temporarily, known as humanitarian parole. Parole does not itself grant immigration status or permanent residence. Initial uncertainty about benefits in the emergency response is historical context, not a rule about current eligibility. Special Immigrant Visa pathways have served Afghans with certain U.S. government or international mission jobs, and eligible family members. Applicants must meet other requirements too. Others came through refugee, asylum or family pathways. Current rules, deadlines and a person’s circumstances require qualified review. The State Department FAQ checked on November 16, 2026, lists a December 31, 2025, deadline for new Chief of Mission applications. This course explains past pathways; it does not guide an application or promise that a route remains open.

For DHS work, the practical point is restraint. Ask immigration questions only for an authorized program purpose, using the current process and required notices. Eligibility staff explain program requirements within their role; individualized immigration legal advice belongs with a qualified attorney or accredited representative. The Minnesota Department of Health (MDH) distinguishes primary arrivals, initially resettled in Minnesota, from secondary arrivals who first resettled elsewhere. Initial resettlement is not necessarily the person’s first physical stop in the United States. Neither arrival series is a complete census of the community.
lessons.keyPoint: Afghan Minnesota includes long-settled families and many people who arrived after the evacuation, through different and changing pathways. Leave status questions to the processes and legal services that need them.
lessons.example: Fictional practice case: Rahela, a DSD program specialist, is preparing an outreach plan for disability waiver information in Hennepin County. A colleague suggests adding a line to the sign-in sheet asking attendees whether they arrived on parole, a Special Immigrant Visa or as refugees, so the team can tailor materials. Rahela notices the outreach session does not determine eligibility for anything. She wonders whether the question will help anyone, and whether it may keep families away.
lessons.question: What should Rahela do about the proposed status question?
choices: Keep the question but make it optional, since optional questions cannot cause harm.
Drop the question and instead ask attendees which language and interpreter they prefer, directing any eligibility questions to the right intake process.
Replace it with a question about which province people came from, which is less sensitive.
feedback: Optional questions still signal what the agency wants to know. At an information session where status serves no purpose, the question can create fear and discourage attendance without improving the service.

This is the strongest choice. Ask for communication needs through an appropriate, private route and explain why the information is needed. Direct eligibility questions to the responsible process; an outreach sign-in sheet is not a status-screening tool.

Province of origin can matter for interpreter matching, but collecting it on a sign-in sheet without a clear purpose is still unnecessary. Ask about language preference directly, and only when it helps the person.
lessons.reflection: Think about a form or intake step you use. Which questions on it are there because a rule requires them, and which are there out of habit?
lessons.action: Review one outreach or intake document you use this week. For each question that touches immigration or origin, write down the rule or purpose that requires it. Flag any question without a purpose and raise it with your supervisor or the program owner.

check.question: Why can state refugee arrival counts understate the size of an Afghan community in a Minnesota county?
check.correct: Primary-arrival counts describe people initially resettled in Minnesota; people who first resettled in another state belong to a separate category, and neither series is a community census.
wrong: They count only people who hold Special Immigrant Visas.
They include only people who have become U.S. citizens.
check.feedback: MDH distinguishes initial resettlement in Minnesota from later moves here after resettlement elsewhere. A transit stop or military-base stay is not the same as a resettlement destination. Arrival data do not measure every resident or later population change.

lessons.title: Languages and peoples: Dari, Pashto and much more
objectives: Identify Dari and Pashto as widely used languages and name other languages Afghan individuals may prefer.
Describe the ethnic diversity of Afghanistan, including Pashtun, Tajik, Hazara, Uzbek and other peoples, and the limits of population estimates.
Explain why a Farsi interpreter may not serve every Dari speaker well.
Plan an interpreter request that asks about language, dialect and comfort.
lessons.teaching:
Dari and Pashto are widely used in Afghanistan and among Afghan newcomers. Article 16 of the 2004 Constitution named both as official languages and recognized specified regional languages. That historical document is not a reliable account of every current governing practice. Afghan people may also speak Uzbek, Turkmen, Baluchi, Nuristani, Pamiri, Hazaragi and other languages. Many people use more than one language. Ask separately about preferred spoken and written communication; schooling history, language familiarity, disability and other circumstances can affect what works.

The country is also ethnically diverse. The largest groups are usually listed as Pashtun, Tajik, Hazara and Uzbek, followed by Turkmen, Baloch, Aimaq, Nuristani and others. Treat any percentages you see with care. The 1979 census was itself incomplete, as the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) explains in its historical account of population-data gaps. Later surveys have varied in coverage and questions. The Minority Rights Group profile also warns that reliable current ethnic population counts are unavailable. Do not present estimates as a precise census or transfer national proportions to Minnesota. Religion is similar: nearly all Afghans are Muslim, most Sunni, with a Shia minority that includes many Hazara. Small Sikh and Hindu communities also have Afghan roots. Ethnicity, region and faith have shaped who was targeted in past conflicts, so these are not neutral topics for everyone.

For language access, the details matter. The Minnesota Department of Health notes that Dari and Farsi are both forms of Persian, but a Dari speaker may or may not understand Farsi well, depending on where they are from. MDH also recommends orienting interpreters to a family's city or province of origin. Less common languages among recent arrivals include Hazaragi and Uzbek. So do not stop at asking whether someone speaks Persian. Ask what language the person prefers, whether a particular dialect matters, and whether they want written material or spoken explanation.

Comfort with a particular interpreter can matter too. A person may prefer an interpreter of a certain gender, or may worry about confidentiality in a small community. Ask these questions of everyone, in a neutral way, rather than assuming what someone wants from their ethnicity or appearance. The person's answer is the guide, not your prediction.
lessons.keyPoint: Ask for the person's preferred language and dialect instead of assuming Farsi, Dari or Pashto. Afghanistan's ethnic and language diversity is real, and estimates of it are uncertain.
lessons.example: Fictional practice case: Joel, a county case manager working with a DSD-funded program, schedules a Farsi interpreter for Marzia, an Afghan woman who is applying for services for her son. During the call, Marzia answers briefly and asks the interpreter to repeat several questions. Afterward the interpreter mentions that some of Marzia's words sounded like Hazaragi. Joel had not asked about language preference beyond the referral form, which said Persian.
lessons.question: What is Joel's best next step?
choices: Continue with Farsi interpreters, since Marzia did not complain and the referral form said Persian.
Ask Marzia's teenage son to interpret next time because he speaks English well.

Use the approved language-access process to confirm Marzia’s preferred language and any dialect or interpreter needs, with qualified assistance. Arrange a suitable interpreter and record only the service-relevant preference under the program’s rules.
feedback: The repeated questions are a reason to check whether communication worked, not proof of a particular dialect or a language mismatch. Ask Marzia directly through appropriate language assistance rather than waiting for a complaint.
Using a child to interpret for a parent in a service discussion about that same child raises accuracy, privacy and family role concerns. Use a qualified interpreter.

This is the strongest choice. It checks Marzia’s preference rather than assigning Hazaragi from another person’s impression. Explain available options and confidentiality arrangements, then verify that the interpreter can support the conversation.
lessons.reflection: When you request an interpreter, what do you usually know about the person's language beyond its general name? What would you need to ask to know more?
lessons.action: Review the interpreter request process and draft prompts about preferred language, dialect and interpreter needs. Share proposed changes with the responsible language-access staff before changing an intake process.

check.question: Why should staff be cautious about precise percentages for Afghanistan's ethnic groups?
check.correct: Available estimates draw on incomplete or differently scoped data, and the 1979 census itself was incomplete; they are not precise counts of today’s population.
wrong: Because all Afghans belong to the same ethnic group.
Because the percentages have been fixed by treaty and cannot change.
check.feedback: UNFPA describes the incomplete 1979 census and later data gaps. Check the source, date and scope of an estimate; national proportions cannot identify an individual or establish Minnesota’s community composition.

lessons.title: Family, gender and communication without stereotypes
objectives: Describe how extended family can shape decisions for many Afghan families while recognizing variation.
Distinguish offering choices about gender and privacy from assuming what a person wants.
Explain how name spelling and date differences can arise in records.
Draft neutral questions about who a person wants involved in a conversation.
lessons.teaching:
Many Afghan families place a high value on extended family. Decisions about health, money or a child's care may involve parents, spouses, older siblings or elders, and people may want relatives present at appointments. That is a pattern, not a rule. Afghan Minnesotans include people from cities and rural areas, people with university degrees and people who had little chance to attend school, people who worked closely with U.S. agencies and people who never did, and families who have lived here for decades alongside people who arrived in the past few years.

Gender is an area where stereotypes can do harm in two directions. Some Afghan women and men prefer a provider or interpreter of the same gender, especially for health or personal topics. Some want a spouse or relative present. Others do not. Many Afghan women were students, teachers, doctors, lawyers and public servants, and the restrictions placed on women's education and work after the Taliban's return affected them sharply. Do not assume a woman cannot speak for herself, and do not assume she wants a relative to speak for her. Ask everyone who they would like involved and whether they have an interpreter preference, including gender. Explain available arrangements and address access needs through the proper process rather than promising a particular interpreter. Speak directly to the person and offer a private conversation when appropriate. A relative’s presence does not itself authorize disclosure, consent or decision-making; check the person’s wishes and any applicable legal authority.

Faith practice varies as well. Many Afghans are observant Muslims and may fast during Ramadan, pray at set times, or prefer halal food, while others practice differently. Scheduling flexibility, such as avoiding meal-time meetings during Ramadan when asked, is a simple courtesy.

Records raise practical issues. Names written in Dari or Pashto script can be spelled several ways in English letters, and a family's members may not share one surname in the way English-language forms expect. Birth dates on documents are sometimes estimates. When records do not match, ask how the person uses their name and follow the program’s identity-verification and correction process. Record relevant variants with their source when permitted. Do not select an official birth date or replace a legal record based only on preference, and do not infer dishonesty from a mismatch.
lessons.keyPoint: Ask about family participation, interpreter needs and privacy, then arrange appropriate support within the person’s choices and applicable authority. A community pattern does not establish an individual preference.
lessons.example: Fictional practice case: Nadia, a DSD grants coordinator, is helping plan a listening session for Afghan parents of children with disabilities. A team member proposes holding separate sessions for mothers and fathers because that is what Afghan families would expect. Another team member worries that would exclude single parents and mothers who want to attend with their husbands. The community partner organization has not yet been asked.
lessons.question: What should Nadia do?
choices: Ask the community partner and varied parents what would help them participate. Plan feasible group and private options, explain available interpreter and facilitator arrangements, and address language and disability access needs.
Hold only separate sessions, since that is the cultural norm for Afghan families.
Hold only a mixed session, since separating by gender would be a stereotype.
feedback: This is the strongest choice. It checks varied preferences and explains what can be arranged. One partner does not speak for every parent, and a private option still needs clear information about confidentiality and use of feedback.
Deciding for the whole community assumes one practice fits everyone. Some parents may prefer mixed sessions, and single parents may be left out.

Rejecting other formats can also exclude people, including parents who would speak more freely in a small or private conversation. Avoiding one stereotype by imposing another format does not solve the problem.
lessons.reflection: Think of a time a routine assumption about family roles shaped a meeting you were part of. What question would have tested that assumption?
lessons.action: Draft a short, neutral script for the start of your next meeting with a family: who they would like present, their interpreter preference, and whether they would like any part of the conversation to be private. Try it with any family, not only Afghan families.

check.question: Which approach best respects variation in gender and family preferences?
check.correct: Ask each person who they want involved and about interpreter needs, explain available options, and follow applicable privacy and decision-making requirements.
wrong: Always direct questions to the oldest man present, since that is the family custom.
Never allow relatives to attend, so that every person speaks for themselves.
check.feedback: Both wrong answers impose a rule without asking the person. Invite preferences and arrange appropriate support; family involvement does not automatically authorize disclosure or decision-making.

lessons.title: Service barriers and respectful practice
objectives: Identify common service barriers reported for Afghan newcomers in Minnesota.
Explain why staff should not ask people to retell evacuation or war experiences.
Distinguish information a service needs from information that is merely interesting.
Plan referrals to resettlement, legal and community resources.
lessons.teaching:
Afghan newcomers in Minnesota met several barriers at once. The account of the state's rapid health response describes an overstretched health system during the pandemic, a weakened resettlement network, and long uncertainty about whether parolees would qualify for federal benefits and health coverage. That account concerns the 2021–2022 response, not the present circumstances of every Afghan Minnesotan. People may face family separation, housing costs, employment barriers, school transitions or grief, and may also have substantial personal and community strengths. Ask what matters to this person rather than assuming a history or a need.

Many Afghans lived through violence, threats and a chaotic evacuation. That does not mean every person is traumatized, and it does not give staff permission to ask about it. Do not ask people to describe how they left Afghanistan, what they saw, or why they were at risk unless a specific, authorized process requires it and trained staff are doing it. Unnecessary questions can cause distress and collect information unrelated to the service. If someone chooses to share, listen and ask how they would like to proceed. Respond to any immediate safety concern through the appropriate process without demanding an account of traumatic events.

The same restraint applies to immigration status. Collect it only when a program rule requires it, and follow the program's instructions for what to ask. Government collection, use and disclosure must follow applicable data practices rules. Give required collection notices, use approved systems and confirm authority before discussing another person’s private information. Marriage or family membership alone is not a blanket authorization. Consult your data practices contact when unsure.

Respectful practice is mostly a set of good questions. What language would you like to use? Who would you like here with you? What is the most important thing we can help with today? Is there anything that would make this easier, such as a different time, a phone call or a woman interpreter? The DHS Resettlement Programs Office and Refugee and Immigrant Helpline can help connect people with services and legal help. The helpline is a navigation and referral service, not a substitute for individualized legal advice. Offer community-led organizations as options and check their current services, eligibility, capacity and language arrangements before promising a referral outcome.
lessons.keyPoint: Meet present needs with good questions, clear referrals and care with data. Do not ask people to retell trauma or disclose immigration status that the service does not require.
lessons.example: Fictional practice case: Omar, a DHS call center specialist, takes a call from Fariba, who arrived with her family in recent years and is asking why her husband's health coverage letter says something different from hers. Omar's colleague suggests he ask how they came to the United States, what happened in Afghanistan, and whether they are still on parole, to better understand the family's situation.
lessons.question: What should Omar do?
choices: Ask about the evacuation first to build rapport and understand the family's background.

Confirm language needs and authority to discuss each person’s information. Review the relevant notice within Omar’s role, explain the stated reason and deadlines, and connect unresolved eligibility or legal questions to the appropriate staff or referral service.
Tell Fariba the difference is probably because of immigration status and suggest she contact a lawyer.
feedback: The evacuation story is not needed to explain a coverage notice and could be distressing. Rapport comes from being helpful and respectful, not from asking for personal history.

This is the strongest choice. Omar must establish what he may access or disclose before comparing spouses’ notices. He should explain the actual reason and any response or appeal deadline, without guessing from nationality or treating a referral as a substitute for timely program action.

The cause cannot be inferred from Fariba’s background. Review authorized information and the notice’s stated reason, or connect her with the responsible staff. Preserve any response or appeal deadline while obtaining help.
lessons.reflection: When a person's story is complex, what helps you stay focused on the question they brought to you?
lessons.action: Find and save the contact information for the DHS Resettlement Programs Office, the Refugee and Immigrant Helpline, and your division's data practices contact. Add them to a referral list you can reach quickly during calls or meetings.

check.question: When is it appropriate for general DHS staff to ask someone to describe what happened during their evacuation or flight?
check.correct: Generally never, unless a specific authorized process requires it and trained staff conduct it; otherwise focus on current needs.
wrong: Always, because understanding trauma helps staff build trust.
Whenever the person seems comfortable enough to talk.
check.feedback: General staff should not seek a traumatic history merely to build rapport. A voluntary disclosure deserves a respectful response, but it does not invite further probing or remove privacy and professional-role limits.

cards.back: Temporary permission to stay in the United States; parole does not itself grant immigration status or permanent residence. Many 2021 evacuees arrived this way. Current benefits and legal options need individual review.
A pathway with specific employment and other requirements for qualifying Afghan applicants and eligible relatives. Historical eligibility does not establish that a new application remains available.
Widely used languages among Afghan newcomers. Dari is a form of Persian; ask about language and dialect rather than assuming a Farsi interpreter is suitable.
A person initially resettled in Minnesota in MDH’s arrival reporting. Secondary arrivals first resettled in another state. Neither category is a complete community census.
Community context helps you ask better questions. It never tells you what an individual believes, wants or has experienced.

aid.heading: Before the conversation
items: Confirm preferred language and dialect, not only Persian or Afghan.
Ask whether the person has an interpreter preference, such as gender.
Check whether the task needs immigration status at all; if not, do not ask.
Allow extra time and offer a phone or in-person option.

aid.heading: During the conversation
items: Ask whom the person wants involved, speak directly to them, and confirm applicable disclosure and decision-making authority.
Offer a private moment when personal topics come up.
Avoid unnecessary questions about war or flight; listen respectfully if someone chooses to share and stay within your role.
Confirm name usage and follow approved identity-verification and correction procedures for mismatched records.

aid.heading: Referral and follow-up
items: Connect immigration legal questions to qualified legal help; the Refugee and Immigrant Helpline can help locate services.
Connect to the DHS Resettlement Programs Office for resettlement services.
Offer Afghan-led community organizations as an option, not a requirement.
Record service-relevant communication preferences under program rules, explain their use and confirm them when needed.

sources.title: Minnesota Department of Health — Minnesota Refugee Health Report 2024
sources.note: Historical 2024 report, including 603 primary arrivals from Afghanistan; not the latest cumulative data or a community census. Relevant indexed report text checked; direct PDF access unavailable.

sources.title: Minnesota Department of Health — Cumulative Refugee Arrivals, 1979–2025
sources.note: Live cumulative file has advanced to 2025 and an indexed Afghan total of 2,923. Do not label it a fixed 1979–2024 table or use it as a current population census.

sources.title: Minnesota Department of Human Services — Resettlement Programs Office
sources.note: Current resettlement-service entry point. Replaces the former Afghan-evacuees page, which no longer returned substantive content during review.

sources.title: Frontiers in Public Health — Welcoming new neighbors: Minnesota's rapid response model to address the urgent health needs of Afghan newcomers, 2021-2022
sources.note: Peer-reviewed account supporting 1,260 evacuees in 386 families, humanitarian parole context, and barriers including benefit uncertainty and a strained system. Describes the early response period only.

sources.title: Minnesota Department of Health — Afghan Clinical Guidance, Center of Excellence in Newcomer Health
sources.note: Supports Dari and Pashto as preferred languages, the Dari and Farsi caution, less common languages such as Hazaragi and Uzbek, and orienting interpreters to province of origin.

sources.title: Minority Rights Group — Afghanistan country profile
sources.note: Historical country background with an explicit warning about ethnic-data reliability. Its publication context predates some later developments; not a current account of government practice.

sources.title: U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services — Information for Afghan Nationals
sources.note: Federal reference retained for Afghan immigration information. Direct access was unavailable during review; current SIV details were checked with the State Department and the general parole distinction with GAO.

sources.title: Minnesota Department of Human Services — Refugee and Immigrant Helpline
sources.note: Verified navigation, referral and language-assistance role; does not establish that a navigator provides immigration legal advice.

sources.title: UNFPA Afghanistan — Linking population, policies and development
sources.note: Historical account confirms the incomplete 1979 census and later survey limits. Displayed publication date is inconsistent with references to 2014; used for historical data context only.

sources.title: U.S. Department of State — Afghan Frequently Asked Questions
sources.note: Current FAQ checked for application deadlines and qualified SIV context. Legal advice and individual eligibility remain outside the course.

sources.title: U.S. Government Accountability Office — Humanitarian Parole, GAO-26-107433
sources.note: Background definition of temporary parole and distinction from admission or immigration status. Findings about other parole programs are not applied to Afghan individuals.

sources.title: Afghanistan Ministry of Justice — 2004 Constitution, Article 16
sources.note: Historical constitutional language provision; not an assertion that the entire 2004 framework governs current practice.

sources.title: Minnesota Statutes 13.05 — Duties of responsible authority
sources.note: Subdivision 3 limits collection and storage to necessary authorized program purposes; subdivision 4 addresses collection, use and disclosure, including informed consent.

sources.title: Minnesota Statutes 13.46 — Welfare data
sources.note: Subdivision 2 makes welfare-system individual data private with specified disclosure routes. Family membership is not a blanket disclosure authorization.
